Content: I'm seeing this video a few days late but, as a person who is also not terribly far from the Eaton fire, it's really scary. I was able to see the fire light from my house and especially from my chruch that I go to. But also coming from the east coast where I've lived my entire life and to be here for about 2 years now, it was crazy, devestating, and you usually hear about fires but it has NEVER been this bad. But, also to a different note, I heard my church was accepting donations and starting a fund the day we had to evacuate that Tuesday or Wendesday. I was exahusted the first day, we came back again, again, and again, and to see how much people really care is remarkable. I also come from places which would be rare to see big kindness and giving but when I helped it made me feel good but I also have survivors guilt. I'm trying my best and still help vollenteer there, we are fully stacked and packed with water, clothes, and food but we can't accept anymore clothes but only clean socks and underwear. I sadly have some friends of mine who have lost their homes and we will help them as much as possible and it's so heartbraking to hear or see peoples devestation. I'm thankful that my house is intacked but like I said before, I feel survivors guilt, and what you/markiplier said before, Rose Bowl had to now turn away people because they're like "We are absolutely FULL on donations, go take them to a different place" and they'd list MANY places. Also knowing that Cali/LA is also the "city of angels" you can see that it's true when you see this much help and I also know that's not just Californians helping, it's other states and I'm sure there might be a few COUNTRIES helping! Content: Back in 2011, my family had to evacuate from fires that were tearing up our street and everywhere around us. We all crammed into my aunt's single bedroom apartment and waited for news for a few days, and then went to another relative's house where I slept in my 10-year-old cousin's bunk bed. Author: @hayleigh6989
Content:
We're glad you're safe and appreciate your big heart, Mark. I've noticed a lot of activists sharing on Instagram the contrast between how the fires have been devastating people and showing images of hospitals and schools in Gaza on fire. I can't imagine the grief and despair people in LA must feel, and that's just a fraction of what Palestinians have been facing for over 460 days. Both are horrific, of course. I think of all of the helpers like you who do what needs to be done. I think of all the doctors, nurses, firefighters (many whom are incarcerated and work for very low wages), and regular folks who do what needs to be done. It's amazing what people will do for each other in disasters like these, just to keep surviving and carrying hope.

I keep thinking about how small my problems feel as an observer while so much suffering is happening globally. Fires like these are predicted to become more frequent with hurricane winds, and it's going to happen more frequently. So much of this destruction could have been avoided with proper funding and prioritization of environmental stewardship. We get forest fires quite often during our summers where I'm from, and it can be jarring anticipating if the same could happen directly in my community. Hell,  we had huge trees uprooted from hurricane winds this summer and some crushed cars and homes. Climate change affects all of us, even if we feel like we're exempt from it. We gotta look out for one another <3

Author: @Jason-eo5bv
Content: I was in the impact zone of Helene in WNC. Strong winds worry me, heavy rain freaks me out a little, creaking trees now carry fear instead of awe, and the sounds of emergency vehicles causes me to become very alert. I still haven't even gone directly down to spots deeply impacted within my area, just from afar, because seeing it up close hurts too much. This was my town, an entire part of it wiped away by water, so many people lost along with everything others had. My heart goes out deeply to California, this is a horrific event and hope everyone remembers to take care of themselves. The biggest suggestion I can make to anyone reading this, PLEASE, take a breather if you're helping Cali out. Like if you're boots on the ground, gathering info, helping hand out food, volunteering at a shelter, whatever it is you NEED to take a break. I burnt out within a week between boots on the ground and helping in what ways I could, it deeply hurt my mental health pushing myself so severely without giving myself the time to laugh, cry, or scream. Remember to breathe please, because the trauma alone will be devastating when it does start hitting, but you really need to let yourself rest so it doesn't hurt worse.

Author: @KyleCorbeau
Content:
0:58 If you have the ability to and are in an area where natural disasters (fires, hurricanes, etc.) happen seasonally/frequently, I would HIGHLY ADVISE to keep an abridged go bag in your car. God forbid you are out and about and something happens to your home you'll at least not be entirely screwed. 

A good starting point I would recommend:
2 Changes of clothes, a reusable water bottle, entertainment that does not require power (highly suggest a book as it can serve dual purpose in true emergencies for a fire starter), a pair of (sturdy) shoes, flashlight with extra batteries, and a blanket. If you have pets, an extra leash, a slip collar, and 2 collapsible bowls as wells (one for food, one for water), and an empty clean gallon container that water could be stored in (bonus if you have water in it already because BOY does that make it a little easier if your radiator goes out). If they're a small pet look into fold flat carriers that could be stored in the pocket behind your driver's seat. 

  Nothing that would destroy you if stolen but could make your life drastically easier if you were unable to get home in time. I know it sound like a lot but I have way more than just that in mine and it takes up the space of a backpack. 👍

Content: Living in Canada I'm more than familiar with seeing wildfires in nearly every direction the past few years. One thing to keep in mind, and is VERY important in particularly dry times, is the risk of holdover fires. Embers underground can go weeks or months before igniting brush on top of it, and california is rich in trees perfect for making up these ember pockets. If you or anyone you know is particularlly close to the fires, keep dead grass, brush or debris clean for a while or consider tilling firebreaks if that's something you have the means to do.

Author: @HiggsMonaghan5
Content:
Hey dude, I hope you’re okay. I went through the (almost) same thing in NC with Hurricane Helene, and we wish you well. You bring joy to us, and NC wishes you well. Stay strong, we in NC are rooting for you. Heres some stories from my family that can help make you feel a little better(it at least helped me feel better when hearing about them from my grandparents)

1. My grandpa’s Uncle Billy’s house was by the river and during Helene, it flooded. Neck deep water. When my grandpa went to go clean it with some marine buddies of his, he ran over a kitchen knife.

2. We lost the camper, but, it was really funny how we lost it. My grandpa, who said that the water wouldn’t get that high, maybe it get into the trailer some and all that stuff, was wrong. The water got up so high it got to the swimming pool, which is really high on the hill. For a bit, the camper became a boat, and my bike was unfortunately lost in the mud and water. 

3. My dad is a Lineman, meaning he fixes powerlines and stuff. During that time in Helene, he saved countless lives with his crew. When he finally returned form it all, he said “(Name), I want you to remember this period of your life because of the countless people lost and the amazing people who saved countless others.”

4. After we returned back to my home in a small town, we learned that across the parking lot, where theres a forest, people tied trees to where they would fall away from peoples cars, so people could get out and leave.

5. During the first day of the storm, me and my grandparents on my dad’s side (who I was with at the time), had been trapped in their trailer, where in the rock and dirt driveway, a massive tree had fallen. If my dad hadn’t left hours earlier, he’d have been trapped with us. Some people had actually came and cut down the tree after the rain had lifted up. After, there were reports of an EF-2 tornado.

6. One of my grandparents’ friends’ brother’s had been trapped in a trailer and washed down a river(that was made by the intense flow of water in Ashville), had been found as someone who was walking around outside trying to see if anyone needed help because there was yelling. He was fine, but unfortunately their grandmother passed away.

I hope these stories help light a fire of warmth inside of the people who are currently in LA that can help or who are being evacuated or anything at all. Love from NC.

Folks need to be made AWARE that if you are in a DISASTER and your home or property is WRECKED or destroyed, be AWARE of PREDATORY CONTRACTORS! We fell victim to one.

Author: @emptysora_
Content:
I… It’s awful what’s going on right now. But, your altruism is one of the biggest things I admire about you. Please stay safe (I say this to everyone in LA, including all the wildlife and other animals). And, please keep us updated, even after mainstream coverage inevitably fades.

I’ll be hoping and praying that the fires don’t spread further into LA—that nobody else, or, rather, as few other people will be forced to suffer. I hope that as few other people need to lose most or everything they own.

But, I will say… I was out of state when the eye of Milton struck just 30 miles south of where I live—our neighborhood was still inside the cone of uncertainty just before landfall. It’s one thing to see photos or videos of the damage. But, to be able to see all the damage in person, it’s absolutely unreal. Even more so when it’s the landmarks and features you see every single day of your life. It’s an indescribable feeling.

And, we are STILL nowhere near cleaned up here in Pinellas County, months later.
Naturally, however, national coverage is all but gone now. I mean, anyone remember Helene? The OTHER major hurricane that hit Florida, the Big Bend region, a mere THIRTEEN days prior to Milton? The near-record-breaking hurricane that devastated Georgia and the Carolinas? Asheville? The dam failures? Cities literally being wiped off the map?
I just… I really don’t want to see that happen with the California wildfires too. Like you mentioned. Sadly, I’m sure it’s inevitable.

It just feels so patronizing, sometimes, the way some outsiders treat the survivors of natural disasters. Like we and everyone else in these kinds of situations are just objects to look at and pity, only to be forgotten when the next disaster survivors are born. It’s disgusting. We’re “victims” to a lot of people, not “survivors”. The recovery gets barely any spotlight at all. So, I’m glad you shared that anecdote.

Author: @ceekay3143
Content:
As an Australian who was once a (volunteer) member of the State Emergency Service, I really feel for you and appreciate how you are trying to help your community. Please make sure you're safe and don't burn yourself out with compassion and chainsawing. Sometimes all you can do is talk with your community, maybe even store things safely for later down the track when donations slow down or houses are rebuilt.

That is the one good thing to come from such horrible and unpredictable natural disasters: they highlight the good in humanity. Hopefully you saw footage of how bad the fires were here 5 years ago; some places have still not recovered from the bushfire-Covid double whammy. We did raise over AU$50 million in charity/relief (that's like $2 a person). Our fire danger rating system has been changed and overhauled. We've even started practising bushfire evacuations and shelter-in-place at schools with higher risk of bushfires (we've always had whole school plans and practice for general evacuation, but not specifically for bushfire scenarios and how we'd get all the kids home, or keep them safe in the hall if it's not safe to leave).

Author: @Charas_Cottage
Content: I was in a big forest fire up where I live, I was in an immediate evac and had to leave right then and there before the traffic and firefighters had to come in. Let me tell you, it was traumatizing. Seeing the skies a dark reddish orange with ash falling down. It was awful, it looked like a post apocolyptic world. Like we had just been nuked. We were evacuated for nearly 3 weeks until we could get home, also, at this time, the power to our house was shut off because of this fire so everything in our fridge was rotted. Things were left out when we were packing. I would have nightmares about being in a fire and the anxiety was just painful at times. I can walk to the huge clearing sites where they had to put the fire powder stuff on the fire, where they had to clear out a huge amount of trees. Its less than a 5 minute walk. I understand how people are feeling and I thank the fire fighters near our house that helped so many people and helped save my house. They atually thanked us for letting them use our creek in front of our house as a water supply. Prayers for the families and people down in LA, and thank you to the fire fighters and emergency people for doing the best they can in times of crisis!! 🥰💖💖

Author: @caelnoyce253
Content:
I'm so relieved to hear you, Amy, and your dogs are okay!! When I heard about the fires, immediately all my favorite parasocial peeps came to mind. I hope everyone else is holding up strong, too. 

While tragedy is a horrible thing to witness and experience, I am so so glad you got to experience the beautiful aftermath of people coming together to rebuild. When I worked the Waynesville, Ohio Renaissance Faire, hurricane Helene tore through our campground with category 1 hurricane winds. The only reason our tent stayed standing is because we physically held it up. People who stayed through the week were running around, trying to protect their stuff, on top of trying to stake tents down and stay on top of the tragedy. It didn't matter how many stakes they put down, the entire campground had tents scattered all about, the festival itself suffered, small businesses suffered. It was devastating, but after all was said and done, the amount of people donating and coming together was beautiful. It's unlike anything I have ever seen. By the end of the week, we had mostly rebuilt upon everything that was lost. Just like you described, we were overflowing with donations, and we kept having to turn people away as well. It brought tears to my eyes to know that you experienced this beautiful good in the world. On the flipside, it crushes me that tragedy like this is the only time I have ever seen us as a people put aside our differences and come together. I hope that if there is anything to be gained from this, it is deep deep healing. My heart goes out to you all.

Author: @min-kn9ny
Content:
I live very close, almost on top, of the San Andreas Fault and honestly speaking, despite going through high magnitude earthquakes that quite literally cracked the land open and seeing all of the damage that can be done in seconds, I still feel thankful that’s what I deal with and not other stuff like hurricanes or fires or anything like that. Because that can be seen from miles away, and can only imagine the stress and fear of seeing it coming closer and closer despite the attempts of stopping it, needing to leave and coming back to see everything gone. An earthquake happens without warning and you can instantly check for damage. But to need to leave and have no idea what your house is going to look like is extremely hard, I imagine. Especially to those who can’t take much with them. A house is just a building, yes, but to many, it’s where they grew up with and saw their kids grow up with and maybe even grandkids now. There’s many loved belongings, emotionally heavy belongings that cannot be taken in these “just take what you NEED” moments. Your children’s drawings, their old clothing you keep for memories, plants you’ve spent years looking after, kitchenware that was gifted by someone who already passed. It’s not the loss of belongings that hurts. It’s the permanent loss of memories, of something that anchored you to a moment in life you loved. That, and the worry of rebuilding yourself with money you might not even be close to having

My heart goes out to everyone that lost anything, no matter how “unimportant”, in these fires. I don’t care if it’s a year-long project of yours that you’ve spent a lot of time and effort and money into, or if it’s just a silly album from an artist you don’t even like anymore but that you bought with your first money as a teenager. All of it matters because you kept it for a reason. And I’m sorry that it was taken from you. I hope you guys stay safe, first and foremost, and that things resolve in the best possible way.

Author: @christinaklein1668
Content:
If you are considering donating to those affected by the fires, from experience I can tell you that the most useful donation is going to be money, followed by absolute essentials like toiletries and shelf-stable food that doesn't need any prepwork. Consider that you're donating to someone who has lost their home and may only have their car, if that - they don't have anywhere to put anything. Basically, it'd be a bit like giving furniture to someone without a house. When we lost our house years ago, we had people trying to donate Christmas decorations and decorative baskets and the like, who were a bit confused and sometimes offended that we were refusing certain items. "Just take them to goodwill if you don't end up needing them!" These folks' hearts were in the right place but I frankly didn't have the emotional or physical energy (or the gas money) to take the leftovers to goodwill for them, and I can be pretty myopic and blunt when I get that way, so I hilariously would ask them to take the remainder to goodwill for me, which would blindside them enough that they agreed because they didn't know what else to say in response. It may feel like an impersonal gift, but the people most affected know what they need the most, and will often know how to best get themselves stabilized as quickly as possible. You don't know who managed to save what or who has certain resources - donating clothing to someone who managed to pack a week of clothing isn't going to help as much as cash for food when they don't know where their next meal is going to come from; and donating food to someone whose food stamps just re-upped isn't going to help as much as donating clothing when they weren't able to return home to grab anything before the fires hit. And if you don't have any spare cash to donate, that's when looking through your cupboards could also be useful. Spare clothing, shelf-stable food (again, no prepwork - nothing that requires an oven or even milk (and in fact, shelf-stable milk is something of a holy grail for food banks as far as I understand because they get a lot of cereal and mac and cheese and such that requires it, so if you've got some of that to spare, grab that first), and toiletries are going to be the first things needed. If you have a tent in the garage that you're pretty sure you're never going to use again, or even a sleeping bag, you might consider donating those as well. And if you're able to, fostering a person's pet while they look for a new place to live can also take a significant part of the burden for them. 

But also, good on you for just going outside and figuring out what you can do to improve conditions immediately where you currently are. That's a fantastic mindset and frankly I hadn't thought to do so when we had windstorms last year and there were branches in the streets afterwards, but now I may do something about them next time.

Imagine how scary it is that you can't run, can't even get out of bed as the fire closes in, and ppl and vehicles were supposed to help you. Family members were stopped from entering fire zones to help. These are not hypotheticals, these are real people who depend upon services or medications or aids that it would otherwise be impossible to live without. There are articles on this but just please keep disabled ppl in mind and make a plan for emergencies regardless of your ability. Make backup plans. Support legislation to help the disabled. Make plans with your disabled neighbors. Ty

Author: @CiaraNíShúilleabháin1990
Content:
Wildfires are absolutely terrifying. I was living in Portugal during the 2017 fires that burned 250km² of land and they came very close to where I was living. The eucalyptus forestry across the road from the end of my driveway was completely burned down. Luckily, my house survived, but it was very close to being destroyed. 
We were away for the day when my friends and I heard that the fire was getting near to where we were living. We immediately rushed back to get our dogs who were still at home. The road back to our house was closed because of the fire, so we had to find an alternative route. We ended up having to hike across the wilderness and through fields to get there. We ran back along the road to where we had left our van and the fire was starting to get really close at that point. The air was full of smoke and the heat was so intense. I've never been as scared as I was that day. We were very lucky to get back out alive. 
I feel so bad for everyone who is currently dealing with the fires in LA. It's terrible to think about all of the people who have lost everything. I hope that everybody is as safe as they can be and I send my best wishes to all who are affected. Massive thanks to all of the firefighters everywhere who help to keep people safe during times like this. They are true heroes. ❤️

Content: In disasters such as this, it's easy to think that rescue services are going to take care of things. The reality is, these disasters often overwhelm our rescue services and it takes a long time for them to get in and help everyone, time that not everyone can afford. Regular people getting out there with their own tools is often what makes the most difference. If you see your neighborhood in need, and you can SAFELY do something to help, get out there and do it. And as difficult as it may be, try not to forget the people once the fires are put out. When Mark says "pick up a hammer" I have no problem envisioning him actually doing so. Content: When Mark touched on talking about seeing the fire through his window it reminded me of this summer (2024). There was a large fire right at the end of my road on the large hill between my road and the place where the majority of my family worked and were at the time.. I remember my mom calling me and telling me to grab the dogs and go with my grandma to her house because our road was shutting down and being terrified, especially because I left my cat behind as well because we couldn't get her carrier in time. It was scary, not being able to call my family and make sure everything was okay because they were busy with making sure guests at their work were okay and helping put the fire out. I remember walking outside my house while on the phone with a friend and seeing the massive smoke clouds above my house. It was terrifying and still scares me.. everything was okay, no building burnt, no people hurt.. but that doesn't make it less scary.. and that was only a small, local fire in my tiny town. I can only imagine how everyone in LA feels right now where houses and buildings are burning down and people are actually hurt. If I could donate, I would, but I'm not able too. I hope everyone and everything turns out okay.

Content:
As someone who lives in the PNW, I’m constantly stressed about having to evacuate. My partner and I always joke that our house needs to burn down so that we can restart because old houses just aren’t it, but insurance companies are a NIGHTMARE to work with.

Having an evacuation bag is great first step, but you also need to have a list of EVERYTHING (brand and all) you have inside your house. And identification numbers and proof of purchase go a loooong way. Water, food, showering stuff, laundry detergent, pet supplies. If you can have at least a week’s worth of essentials to go at a moment’s notice, then you’ll do relatively okay.

What donation places need is money, honestly. Being able to purchase what they need directly, and pay their volunteers a stipend for their help goes a long way.

I grew up in Colorado, I'm no stranger to fire but the closest one I've ever been through was right across the street. Someone had been riding a motorcycle and crashed, catching the media of grass on that side of the road on fire and it spread fast.
I was four, I remember seeing the smoke outside and watching my mom (who was the only adult in the house) start pulling pictures off the walls and grabbing the fire safes. At the time I was only upset that the cookies we just made were going to be cold when we came back but now looking back on it as an adult I can't begin to imagine the anxiety my mom must had been feeling scrambling to put everything like pictures and important documents in the truck while also keeping my younger brother and I calm knowing that if the wind changed she might only have minutes to get us in the truck. I don't envy that feeling and now growing up with bigger and bigger fires I've gone through my own evacuation plans in my head every time there's even the slightest risk for my area.

Author: @SeaBlueJay
Content:
It was February 2011, my sister was celebrating her 6th birthday. Only a few seconds after she blew out her candles some of the adults saw smoke in the distance.

Before I could even register what was happening everyone was leaving, my family was grabbing everything important and putting us the car with the dogs. We had to drop my brother's friend off at his house before we could leave, his mate lived only a few houses behind us. The entire street his house was on was red. You couldn't see anything it was all red, I still remember it all these years later.

We went to a family members home and my Dad went back to do what he could to save the house he built with my Mum only 5 years ago at the time.

Our house ended up surviving the fire, but my mate lost everything. She only lived three houses behind me. Everything was gone.

I never fully recovered from that. When we moved house in 2013 my Dad became a volunteer fire fighter for the local fire department. Since then our house has been threatened by fire twice. It's truly terrifying, especially since we have so many animals including chickens. The only way to save them is to set them free and hope they come back. I fear it, every time I smell smoke. 

To all those affected by the LA fires I'm sorry. It's awful. Losing everything. I hope you were at least able to get out safely and that you had time to prepare.

To everyone who lives in a climate that has high chances of fire, please have a fire action plan. My family has empty crates in the shed just in case we need to shove shit in them and go. We know what to do if the worst happens and I recommend you do the same. Prepare for the worst and hope you'll never need it.

Seeing the fire come over the hill next to the area that I live in was scary. And it was burning FAST too, because of the sever droughts that happen every year. (I predict this year is going to be awful for fires again, since we did NOT get a lot of rain this winter). My fiancé and I grabbed our two cats, their food and litter box. We unplugged our PC towers and took those with us. I gathered several days worth of cloths and any medical stuff (Band-Aids, ibuprofen, etc.) that we had and threw it all into a big suitcase I had and went over to my mother in laws place, which was located in the center of town. We stayed there for a night, but thankfully the fire was under control so we were able to go back the next day. Thank gawd the wind had died down or else our house could have easily been utterly destroyed. We watched on Watch Duty and on the news about how the fire had jumped the 4/4 lane highway and were scared to death that we would go back to cinders. Watching, as we drove by, police officers at the SPCA packing their cop cars and suvs with shelter animals was heart wrenching. I live near a prison too, and the inmates had to be evacuated as well. It was terrifying.

Thank you Mark, for taking the time to help your neighbors, and for watching out for their properties. I feel like corporations swooping in to take advantage of people in need is a severely overlooked issue, so thank you for talking about it. I'm not a religious person, but GOD BLESS all the firefighters, Police, EMTs, volunteers, and other emergency personnel that have been helping get people and pets to safety. <3 Real heroes don't ware capes, they wear uniforms.

Author: @branana_b
Content: I live in an area where wind is known to easily reach 60-80mph, sometimes even 90-100mph. The day after Christmas in 2021, a town about 15-20 minutes away from where I live had a massive fire. From my kitchen window we have a clear view of the houses across the field from us, and behind those a major highway and the plains. We watched the fire grow from a small one to burn down nearly the entire plains and into the town about 15-20 mins away from us. My brother’s best friend watched his neighborhood burn down on live TV; they had pretty much no warning because the fire caught up to them so fast. If the winds had blown the other way that day, my house would’ve been gone. In 2022, another fire broke out on a trail next to a weather station/science museum place about 10mins from my house. My parents were coming back from a trip and my brother and I were frantically tossing clothes, personal belongings, and important documents into every duffle bag and backpack we could find. Luckily we had more warning but it was still absolutely terrifying; thankfully it’s the only time we’ve ever had to evacuate. Fire is no joke where I live and it’s scary as hell. So glad to hear you’re okay. I’ve been glued to the news since the fires started; hopefully they’ll get under control soon. My thoughts are with you and the rest of California. Sending love from Colorado. ❤

Author: @QuaziInc
Content:
Don't Get disheartened if you apply to volunteer with certain charities to help during the active emergency, and are rejected. It isn't that they don't want help but often there is a lot of work that goes into preparing a skilled volunteer to work with a charity and its impacted individuals. Your desire to help is appreciated and can be useful for other activities in your community, but having a shelter support billeting food and shower facilities with random strangers is a risk for vulnerable populations that we can't just take anyone who walks in and put them to work. 

What you can do if you aren't interested in donating money, is checking what these shelters are advocating for that aren't being filled or serviced by the relief agencies. niceties like gift cards to allow evacuees to get new clothing that isn't from a pile of used,  unopened boxed toys for kids to open, packages of unopened sanitary pads and feminine hygiene products that can be dispersed at these locations.

Smaller community groups are also more likely to work with larger relief efforts like kitchens making fresh cooked food from religious groups like temples and mosques frequently cook to feed, and need help.

Content:
I remember that I happened to be watching one of ypur videos for the first time, and when I took a break to go outside; THE 2018 OREGON FIRES.
😂😅😮

Edit: I try to joke about it, but... Fuck, this is such a heavy thing.
I'm actually shaking a little while remembering this.
I realized spmething recently; Mark, you inspired me to be a person who makes other people feel better when they're having a bad day. It may not always go through, but the sentiment is there, and it really matters. I've learned so much about myself and life in general, and if I hadn't had both of those things happen in such a short time, I don't know how I would be today.

I am SO proud of you. Not just as a person, but as a figure of ... Real. Reminding me that each post, each hate comment, each passion project, each meaningless clickbait video, each plead for donation in the world- there is a PERSON. Behind the screen. We each have our own lives, our own hopes, shame, confusion, and triumphs, and nothing in life is supposed to be a straight line.

I had a nightmare about you a few years ago; you were coming off-stage, and I was quietly waving hi, not wanting to bother you as I passed by, and you pulled me aside, away from the cameras, and a few sentences that amounted to very adamantly telling me "No one cares." And I woke up smiling. Because I knew that (dream) you were right: It doesn't matter what ypur situation in life is, or how hidden or famous you are, because we are ALL strangers in a world of public life. Everyone needs help at some point, and I urge you to take a break.

I mean this platonically, with a full heart;
Love, we're not going anywhere.
Even if the internet suddenly vanishes for good, there are still so many people, like you, who simply love. The instinct to help others, regardless of any anxiety will ALWAYS pull you to someone who needs it.

I couldn't care less about youtube, or content, or money, or whatever.

At the end of the day, it's people that matter, and you remind me of that.
Thank  you, mark. You mean the heart of the world to me.
❤

Author: @raine4736
Content:
Important reminder during ANY evacuation (I personally live in a major Earthquake zone) - do not forget these things:

- Bottled water/clean drinking water
- Pet food if you have pets (canned preferably)
- Important medicine (seizure/other important body/epipen/insulin)
- Thick shoes/socks
- An emergency radio/crank radio - do NOT bring one that will need to be charged or have batteries swapped frequently.

These are things often forgotten in in-home evac kits. Of course variations apply for situations/environments.

Author: @xXNibiNoNekoXx
Content: I live in BC, Canada, and been having fires every year since I was a small child (the big one of memory in the past being in 2003). Last year multiple towns almost erased, some which family lives. There's nothing more chilling and apocalyptic then seeing the sky grey, with an incomprehensible giant smoke cloud that makes the mountains look small and the whole mountain side is red. The next day everything was greyed out and ash and embers were raining everywhere starting pop up fires throughout the city. People were running around with hoses doing their best. It's just getting worse every year. Keep an eye out for people up to no good, looters happen every time where people are evacuated from. All you can do is support your neighbours, community makes the pain not as sharp.

Author: @shyeahright
Content:
I am so glad that you and yours are safe. For anyone being affected - I have been a responder at the state level. PLEASE DO NOT take THINGS to the response. We know your heart is in the right place, but we need you to understand what happens when you do: we have to pull people away from response in order to accept and inventory things that are brought. We have to find space for them. And in the end, we cannot use them. We have specific rules and regs in place for how we distribute things to the public, and they are there for very good reasons. 
So what CAN you do?
Look for local organizations that are responding and find out how to donate FUNDS. Government reimbursement takes TIME and local government will be depleted. We rely so much on local groups and volunteers. 
Find out where to SIGN UP to volunteer. Please don’t just show up! I know the instinct is strong to do what you can, but we need to make sure we’re keeping track of who is coming and going in and out of different response areas. This is for your safety AND ours. 

And THANK YOU to everyone that keeps checking in, and letting us all know you’re safe. Keep communicating!

Author: @mossthealien
Content:
Had my family's historical house (circa 1890) burn to the ground at the start of 2020 (yeah, it was an extra shitty year for us; imagine what rebuilding mid-global shutdown was like 😊) so I can absolutely empathize with the soul-wrenching heartbreak of losing such a special estate. It will never be the same, even if you manage to put together a similar floor plan.

The secret drawer hidden in the wall panel is gone. All the sentimental band tees and video game collections older than you are gone. The vinyl records. A beloved pet that refused to leave the crawl space no matter what you did as was never seen again. The birth certificates you didn't even think about that didn't survive in the safe... where was the safe? It didn't make it either. The charm of eras past that can never be recreated quite right, not that most contractors would even be willing to try because that would be way out of your budget so you have to settle for some ugly modern farmhouse that has all the personality and grace of a sack of onions. A home people never lived in, just a house someone sold. Wishing it was still here so you might feel happy the way you used to when coming home but can't anymore because nothing here is home or familiar or loved or warm. Just another corporate matchstick ozempic house with a boring roof, and boring windows, and a frame of lumber from trees cut down miles from here, and no soul of its own.

I understand. I hope the healing is easier on you guys than it has been on me. Save a few bricks from the chimney. The contractors took all ours away before I thought to take some. May you all be safe and find home again. I haven't.

Author: @Crisjola
Content:
As a Floridian who ran into major issues by being in the panhandle with Hurricane Michael, it’s beyond appreciated that you’re mentioning the companies that can come in and buy land and former homes for nothing. Mexico City beach was erased completely by the storm (foundations, if that) and now it’s got condos and high rises and it was heartbreaking to watch. My town is 50 miles inland from the coast and 30-100 years ago was logged, with either being let to wild or owned by farmers. They lost their entire lively hood when Michael hit because the whole storm behaved as a tornado and twisted the trees into things that couldn’t be used as solid wood pine. It being such a timber filled mess of a county and town, we didn’t get the bigger companies but we did run into false relief efforts and scammers who over charged to fix homes and clear multi hundred year old oaks that had been torn out of the ground.

My heart goes out to those who lost their entire neighborhoods and everything else. I’m glad that this is remaining in enough of the news, as it should, that you guys have relief efforts locally still occurring. Good luck! And I think a lot of Floridians who understand that this isn’t “just a Hollywood thing” have you and the people of CA’s back.

Author: @jackf1215
Content:
The fact that our school district, LAUSD, has only closed most schools for last Thursday and Friday, as well as only really cancelling school completely in the areas that have been DIRECTLY impacted by the fires themselves is just ridiculous. For me, we are able to smell smoke, see flames, and are at constant risk of evacuation, and I STILL have to wake up at 6 just to go to school this week as if nothing is wrong. This, as well as the fact that another windstorm is happening tonight, is only going to make things worse for literally everyone who has to go to school in these areas—not ones that are currently being doused in flames, but the ones being affected by the fire themselves—is just absurd. The worst part is this: some of my classmates that I know have literally talked about their friends having their houses burned down, and they are still having to come to school, with nowhere to live, currently camped out in their cars. They. Are. Still. Supposed. To. Go. To. School. Because. Their. School. Is. Farther. Away. From. The. Fires.

Imagine how awful that is?! Imagine having everything you know be destroyed, only for LAUSD to brush it off, telling someone who has no home and nowhere to go to just go to school every day as if nothing is wrong? 

Cancelling school last Thursday and Friday wasn’t enough, and we are still being tortured with the constant threat of having our houses and lives destroyed. As I was typing this, I got a message about submitting baby photos for our yearbook. Yeah, thanks, that’s gonna fix this issue. How about we do that instead of temporarily shutting down schools and supplying vulnerable students with some sort of aid? 

We’re finished.

Author: @metisdeer8760
Content:
First and foremost. I am going to say I am glad you're okay. Fires are... something you can't argue with, only something you can get out of the way of.

That said? Have you recently maybe checked Wikipedia for major California fires? I got a front row seat for the fire complex of 2008 in California. I know of people who lost, or were evacuated for the Mendocino Complex, the Rush Fire, the Carr fire, the Monument Fire, the Lava Fire, the Caldon Fire, and countless others which took place in northern California. Northern California has been suffering for decades. On the one hand, many of us are relieved that it's finally getting attention. On the other hand? I am going to say the hard part out loud, so pay attention - the only reason this fire is getting the publicity that it is? Is because it ripped through the rich folks part of town. I say that with having had to help with and watch years of heartbreak, tears, broken dreams, and ash smeared across faces. Lives ruined. Homes destroyed. It's a first for many of you down there, I get it. But for others in your state? It's a horrifying norm.

Content: I’m glad to see you guys are safe Mark, and I respect you for helping your neighbors as well. I’m from the foothills of Appalachia and all I can think of when hearing about the fires is the devastation of Hurricane Helene back in September/October. And unfortunately with the media attention moving away, donations and aid will decrease with it (pro tip for anyone reading this: the best time to give to these causes is up to three weeks later, not always immediately because of things like lack of information and safely mobilizing resources and volunteers etc). For these fires, I’ve just been rounding up at grocery stores that ask at checkout which isn’t much I know but it’s what I’m able to give at the time. Again, I respect you and how charitable and generous you’ve always been and how your first action was to help your neighborhood. My thoughts and prayers are with those affected and displaced by this disaster.

Author: @boazsolorio7744
Content:
I've been a fan of your work for years man, I appreciate everything you're doing in the middle of this. Shouting out Altadena that way is immensely helpful too, especially knowing the weird stereotypes this place is getting. 

My fiancee and I are working on a project (2025 Urban Wildlife Wildfire Response in L.A. County on Native Land) to survey the wildlife taking refuge from the fires that requires community to upload observations of said refugees. We conduct this project through an app called iNaturalist, which is used to gather observations of wildlife and to translate to usable data for scientists.

In the midst of the fires, there are people making uploads all around Los Angeles, which is super helpful given we have a concrete map of which species are found where, so we have a good idea how to restore habitat, notice displaced animals, and organize depending on order of urgency during these fires.

Wanted to put this out there if anyone is interested in participating, but overall keep yourselves safe first.

Thanks so much Mark!

Author: @LXCKE
Content:
Mark, as someone who was dead center in the eye of Hurricane Helene when it hit Asheville North Carolina, my family and I were trapped in our home with minimal access to supplies, no cell service, and no way to evacuate. It was people like you, who went out into the fray with their own equipment, who saved us. So, with all my heart, THANK YOU for doing what you did, and I am so sorry that your area is being afflicted with such devastation. You're experiencing nearly exactly what happened to me in terms of seeing such good will come from the community and seeing entire areas erased from home. The animal shelters were packed with displaced pets; donation centers that were packed. Hell, even McDonalds set up and was giving out free meals to people, which provided my first hot meal in weeks at the time. Thank you so much for putting back into the disaster zone. I know you're going to tell yourself that you're strong and you're fine but seeing this kind of shit and having such a close call with losing everything you have and know, is hard on the mind. Go find a resource for yourself in terms of mental health; talking about it will help.

Please tell all your stories! I look forward to listening.

Love from AVL,
- LOCKE

This happened in the wake of hurricane Fiona. Where I live the worst of it hit saturday night. Most of the city lost power. I also volunteer with a group called Sunday Suppers, its a basically a soup kitchen, we run it differently but you get the idea.

Author: @shadowreaperjb
Content:
not an expert on these things, but I think, is nothing else, clear as much as you can from you property, dry brush, bushes, ect. The less of that that's there, the slower the fire will be passing your property. 

if there's non-emergency fire advice lines in a different city/county you can contact, ask if they have any advice for what to do to get you property and neighbourhood ready (either for the next time, or if this time picks back up. 

Once this has calmed down, maybe reach out to your local fire department and ask if there's any civilian training that they do.

if you or your neighbours have a basement that could survive a fire, work out an emergency storage network. critical documents, or small mementos that would be beyond irreplicable, and get them secured the second a hit of trouble comes up. You should not be worrying about loosing them during the evac order.

Make sure all your neighbours have a go bag, if they don't, or they're likely to need help grabbing it and going, give them a hand. make sure that your neighbour are ready.

community in these situations is really helpful, so it might be worth organising a street rendezvous, somewhere you can all meet after evacing to do a head count and possibly camp out till you get the all clear. This also has the benefit of giving some relief to the shelters, as long as your keeping in touch with authorities while doing it.

Author: @jister804
Content:
It’s so good to hear that you and your family are safe from the initial fire!

My aunt lives(ed) in Altadena and was one of the first houses to be hit by the Eaton fire. Looking back now, we’re lucky that she was just able to get out alive since she was in the worst situation she could’ve been in: 

She’s in her late 60s, lives alone, has night vision issues, her house was completely out of power, and she only knew that a fire was coming at her house when she happened to look out her kitchen window that faced the east. She literally had minutes to scramble for any important papers that were immediately on hand, what she was wearing, and an extra set of clothes before getting to her car and then not being able to get out of her driveway because the road was blocked with cars. She also had to leave her cat behind because she couldn’t find her in the house within such a small window of time. 

When she drove back to her house the next day, it was gone, completely burnt to the ground. She’s lived in that house for over 20 years, and it has been a centerpiece for family gatherings and holiday events for everyone in our family. And the worst part is, she lost all of whatever family photos/mementos she had; because she’s of an older generation, her photos weren’t digitized yet, so she only has a handful on her phone and whatever else other family members/friends can find and share with her.  

She’s been through enough in her life, with her husband passing tragically, going through cancer, and now her house burning down, so I’m so glad that you brought up the people who use tragedies like this to take advantage of victims because, as you mentioned, we’re just waiting for her to be screwed over once more by whatever insurance companies who want to give the least possible monetary amount to as many people as they can.

But again, trying to find any light in this situation, we’re just happy that she got out at all and that she is able to stay with family members for a while. 

I know that so many people lost their own lives or those of family members/pets, and I’m just so incredibly sorry for it. This is just a horrific event that had the absolute worst combination of contributing factors (fire + 100 mph wind, dry land, densely-populated areas, lack of resources for adequate response).

My heart is with everyone affected and I hope that you stay as safe and prepared as you can for any future developments.

❤

Author: @SherrifOfNottingham
Content:
One thing that is SUPER important when you decide you want to help a place hit by a disaster like this.

Leave the initial response entirely to the professionals, you're not a fire fighter so you shouldn't be fighting the fire. You're not a licensed carpenter so don't offer your services to fix broken buildings, you're not a logistics expert so don't start dropping off supplies and materials in random locations.

If you think you have a skill or resource worth giving, contact the local authorities or response teams and tell them what you have to offer, otherwise... all you can do is open your wallet... do be careful of just throwing your money at somebody that says they're a charity to help victims of the fire, it's pretty easy to set up a pretty legit looking campaign that is just trying to profit off of your good will and the disaster.

He's 100% right that the most important thing you can do is to file this disaster into the public's long term memory, the new years earth quake in Japan has basically been forgotten by most people, all of the people that wanted to help when the roads were closed making it impossible to help have moved on and thought "everything has returned to normal" but most of the buildings are still collapsed into the streets. So the best thing you can do is not forget that people will still need help through the rest of this year and for many years to come.

Content:
We had our house burn down too, in 2013 I think it was. It was a basic double wide mobile home type, nothing super fancy, but we lived in that house for well over 10 years. At that point, Dad tried to put the fire out, but because the house went up the ONE year in several years that temperatures got so low to the point of below freezing in Alamama, our water hose was frozen solid. We evacted, and had to watch the house go from a stones throw away from the window of my grandmothers house, who lives with us on the property. Everything, pictures and all decades old up in flames. 

Long story short, after it all went down the support we got from the community was huge. We got donations from all sorts of people, shoes, cloths, toothpaste, etc. I even had a few old high school friends I hadn't seen in years stop by to see how we were doing. Author: @PsychofileIndustries
Content:
Thankyou for preparing and running when told to run. 

I'm a survivor of the Mendocino Complex and something people don't count on the fact that they will shut down escape routes if fires come too close to them. We escaped shortly before they shut down the highways...

Sometimes traffic becomes gridlocked like what happened in the Paradise fire... One of my best friends parents lived in paradise and only knew the fire was on their doorstep because her father received a phone call from her sister asking if he knew about the fire approaching them. He looked outside and a palm tree was on fire in their back yard.

They fled in nothing but their sleep clothes. He didn't even grab his dentures... But they didn't get trapped om the road like so many other terrified souls did... 

Another dear friend of mine lost her home, her property, her clothes and even one of her cats in the ranch portion of the mendocino complex... But she and her parents escaped with their lives. 

Recovery is possible if you are still standing.

Please run. Always run. Fire moves so fast and consumes everything it touches. Appreciate your stuff while it's here but if you live in California, you have to be ready to say goodbye to it all if it means your life is safe. My love to everyone who lived through this and strength for all who are about to recover from it ❤

Author: @Nellethiel
Content:
I live in Butte County, where the Park Fire (429,603 acres) started this summer and where the Camp Fire (153,336) leveled the town of Paradise and killed at least 85 people in 2018. The feeling of getting an evacuation order in the middle of the night is scary but sadly well-known around here. Seeing an active wildfire burning toward your home and wondering if it'll be stopped in time is uncomfortably familiar.

All this is to say that I have an idea of what you've just been through, Mark, and it's AWFUL, and I'm so sorry. The twitchy need to keep refreshing WatchDuty, the gymnastics your stomach does every time you get any kind of Emergency Alert on your phone... those things stick with you.

Thank you also for reminding people about keeping the flow of support going after the primary emergency is averted. People in my area are still struggling to recover from the Camp Fire six years down the road. We all need to look out for each other as best we can!

Content: Remember, if you want to donate items/food always check online what the organisation you are donating to actually requested! Do NOT donate food that can spoil in less than month or two, requires full kitchen or multiple "raw" ingredients to make. We are talking about people who do not have storage place anymore, they lost their homes. DO donate personal hygiene products, dippers, wipes, pads ect. canned and other non perishable foods, baby food and water bottles. Heavy objects and clothes also aren't adviced unless the organisation says otherwise. Some organisations asked for dog food, some for blankets and clothes, some for air mattresses, one even asked for microwaves. Like I said, check before you donate.

Content: In my city (different country) a few months ago we had a huge amount of fires spreading, the city was surrounded. I wasnt in my city at the time but my family was and they were prepared to evacuate because there was a fire right next to our house. You dont understand the full panic until it happens to you, until you or a loved one is at risk. I found out hours later and was so worried because no one was answering the phone, i was crying, i had no idea what to do. I can’t even begin to imagine what its like there in LA, because the fires are much much bigger and have been spreading much faster. I cant even begin to understand how these families feel to be in constant fear that they will have to leave everything behind or risk being taken with the fire. I cant even begin to imagine what family members who dont live in LA but are seeing this go down worry for their friends and family. If you live in the US and in LA or near LA, please do what you can to help these people. You may not understand what its like to be in a situation like that but your help is crucial to these people who are now anxiety ridden, scared, in shock, saddened and just miserable to be in a situation like this. Even if all you can do is talk about the situation and keep an eye on updates that already amazing help to keep this situation in the public eye. I dont even comment a lot but this is something i cant help but sympathize, because i know the fear that comes with this. Please help with whatever it is you can

Author: @szariq7338
Content:
Sadly fires are just the worst kind of natural disaster, simply because it's so hard to counter them. You can prepare your house for a tornado, for a flood, but not for a fire.
We had to deal with a flood in Poland couple of months ago and locals have explicitly said: logistics centers had no idea, what to send where. There was a story of when a truck came with a pallet of bottled water and just dropped it off near the church not knowing what to do with it, as well as people not knowing if they're allowed to touch it or not. That's why you Mark can help your community by finding out, what your area needs the most and tell that to distribution centers.
And advice for others: if you're not relatively close to the disaster site, but not affected, do NOT send the basic aid (like food and water), otherwise you'll clog the logistics. Instead get to know, what kind of harder to get gear people need and buy that instead (e.g. power generators, power tools etc.).

Content: Glad you and your neighborhood are mostly safe for now. It’s so nice to know that there are so many people volunteering and donating to those in need. No matter how hard you may try to help protect yourself or others, there is always some assholes who ruin it. And you may think you are safer from bad people away from civilization but it can make you more vulnerable. Hope this situation comes to an end soon.

Author: @fakjbf3129
Content: For people who want to contribute, money is way more effective than stuff for donations. When 1,000 people all donate items it is a massive logistical overhead to inventory, store and distribute those items plus they will inevitably have an oversupply of some items and an undersupply of others. If those 1,000 people instead donate money the charity can buy supplies in bulk for a discount, they know exactly what they have and what they need, and it will come is set packaging that they can develop systems for handling. It simplifies the logistics immensely and allows the charity to focus on getting the items to the people who need them.
